## Results

Figure 1a illustrates a schematic diagram of MIR upconversion processes in the NbOI flake. Bulk NbOI crystals belong to the monoclinic space group C2 and feature a characteristic van der Waals layered structure along the a-axis (Fig. 1b)28. Figure 1c presents an optical image and an atomic force microscopic image (AFM) of the NbOI flake with a typical thickness of ~8 nm. Atomic-resolved annular dark field-scanning transmission electron microscopy (ADF-STEM) technique confirms the b-axis of the NbOI crystal, consistent with the simulated image (Supplementary Fig. S1c). While NbOI crystals exhibit anisotropic absorption along the two in-plane axes28, no experimental data on absorption in the MIR region was previously available. We measured the absorption spectra of a 20-nm NbOI flake, revealing smooth absorption across a 1000 to 2600 nm spectral range. Notably, the absorption exhibits strong anisotropy in the infrared region (Fig. 1d), attributed to excitonic-absorption-induced decay differences along the two in-plane axes in the visible spectral region28. The difference in the Raman spectra along the b- and c-axes also indicates the anisotropic phonon response derived from different crystal orientations between the two axes (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Strong SHG and THG processes with polarization anisotropy in asymmetric NbOI crystals

We investigate the second- and third-order nonlinear effects of the NbOI crystal in the infrared region through SHG and THG processes (Fig. 2a). The second- and third-order nonlinear susceptibilities of NbOI are quantitatively determined to characterize its nonlinear optical properties. The 𝜒(2) values of the NbOI crystal are calculated to be 147 pm/V at 1300 nm and 121 pm/V at 1700 nm by comparing with quartz (Supplementary Fig. S3). The 𝜒(2) value at 2500 nm is estimated to be ~60 pm/V. The 𝜒(3) values of the NbOI crystal are calculated to be 3×10-19 m2/V2 and 5.5×10-19 m2/V2 at 1550 nm by comparing with the silica substrate and monolayer WS , respectively (Supplementary Fig. S4). The difference in 𝜒(3) is mainly derived from the discrepancies in experimentally reported 𝜒(3) values for TEMDC monolayers. In addition, 𝜒(3) is also independent on the excitation intensity, indicating that extracted 𝜒(3) is not affected by thermal nonlinear optical effects (Supplementary Fig. S5). The SHG (𝜂 = 𝐼 ⁄𝐼 ) and THG (𝜂 = 𝐼 ⁄𝐼 ) conversion efficiencies as a function of the excitation intensity are shown in Fig. 2b. The SHG conversion efficiency under 2500-nm excitation is calculated to be 4.3×10-6 under an excitation intensity of 70 GW/cm2, corresponding to a normalized conversion efficiency (𝜂 ) of 8.6×10-4 W-1 based on the equation34,35: 𝜂 = 𝐼 ⁄𝐼 2. This value is comparable to that of Weyl Te in the MIR region35 and is an order of magnitude higher than that achieved in lithium niobate waveguides34.

The NbOI crystal also exhibits polarization-dependent SHG and THG responses, arising from its intrinsically asymmetric in-plane crystal structure. We introduce the anisotropic ratio (𝜌) to characterize the anisotropic nonlinear optical response of the NbOI crystal. The SHG anisotropic ratio of the NbOI crystal is defined as: 𝜌 = 𝐼 ⁄𝐼 ∝(𝜒 (2) ⁄𝜒 (2) )2 , where 𝐼 is the SHG intensity with the excitation polarization along the (c) x-axis, 𝐼 is the SHG intensity with the excitation polarization along the (b) y-axis. Figure 2c demonstrates polar plot of the SHG intensity under 2500-nm excitation with both parallel and perpendicular configurations. The SHG response demonstrates distinct in-plane anisotropy, with the maximum intensity observed along the b-axis. This observation is well explained and fitted through crystal symmetry analysis of the NbOI crystal (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Note S2). The 𝜌 value at 2500 nm is ~14, corresponding to 𝜒 :𝜒 =3.7. The differences in 𝜌 across different wavelengths arise from the dispersion of the nonlinear optical susceptibility in the NbOI crystal (Fig. 2e, Supplementary Fig. 6b, c, Fig. S9)28. Supplementary Fig. S8a-c show SHG mappings of the NbOI flake at 1400 nm along the b- and c-axes, respectively. Notably, a strong SHG signal is observed when the excitation polarization is along the b-axis, whereas the SHG signal is negligible when the excitation polarization is along the c-axis.

The THG anisotropic ratio is defined as: 𝜌 = 𝐼 ⁄ 𝐼 ∝(𝜒 (3) ⁄𝜒 (3) )2 . Figure 2d demonstrates x- and y- components of the THG intensity under 2500-nm excitation. It can be found that THG intensity is the largest when the excitation polarization is along the b-axis. The extracted relative magnitudes of the 𝜒(3) tensor components are 𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) =1:1.6:0.05:0.2, corresponding to 𝜌 =2.56. THG shows different polar-plot patterns under 1300-nm and 1550-nm excitations due to the 𝜒(3) dispersion (Supplementary Fig. S7). The extracted relative magnitudes of the 𝜒(3) tensor components are 𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) =1:3.2:0.9:0.1 at 1300 nm corresponding to 𝜌 =10 and 𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) =1:0.8:0.9:0.1 at 1550 nm corresponding to 𝜌 =0.64. The anisotropic ratios of SHG and THG as a function of the excitation wavelength in the NbOI crystal are also studied. Figure 2e presents the 𝜌 value depending on the excitation wavelength across a range of 850 to 3200 nm. We find that a 20-nm NbOI flake exhibits a high 𝜌 value of ~10 across a broad spectral range (1300-3200 nm), reaching a value of ~33 under 1400-nm excitation. This behavior correlates well with anisotropic SHG spectra shown in Supplementary Fig. S9a-e. The broad spectral range is larger than those in all the 2D layered materials (Supplementary Table S1). It is worth noting that the 𝜌 value starts to decrease from 10 at ~850 nm to the minimum value of 1 at ~1070 nm, which corresponds to the exciton peaks P /P at ~530 nm along the c-axis. Exciton peaks P /P enhance the SHG intensity along c-axis, while reducing the SHG anisotropy at ~1070 nm.

Figure 2f illustrates the 𝜌 value as a function of the excitation wavelength ranging from 1250 to 2600 nm, corresponding to anisotropic THG spectra in Fig. S9f-j. NbOI exhibits a high 𝜌 value of ~17, which gradually decreases at wavelengths beyond 1250 nm. Strikingly, the 𝜌 value exhibits a transition (𝜌 < 1 ) and reaches a minimum value of ~0.38 when the excitation wavelength approaches 1590 nm. The corresponding THG wavelength aligns with the P /P exciton peaks at ~530 nm along the c-axis28, where three-photon enhancement along the c-axis contributes to wavelength-dependent changes in THG anisotropy. Furthermore, THG mappings of the NbOI flake at 1300 nm are also performed for linear polarization parallel to the b- and c-axes, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S8d-f). The mapping intensity in Fig. S8e is larger than that in Fig. S8f, confirming strong THG anisotropy at 1300 nm. This mapping technique enables effective identification of the crystal axes in large-area NbOI flakes. The 𝜌 value of ~17 is higher than that observed in most reported 2D layered materials (Supplementary Table S2).

High-order harmonic processes

Due to the inversion symmetry breaking caused by spontaneous ferroelectric polarization in the bulk state, even-order harmonic processes (such as SHG, SFG, 4th-, and 6th-harmonic processes in the MIR region) can be potentially realized in the NbOI flake28,36. The high-order multiphoton optical processes in NbOI flakes are investigated based on a home-built optical system (Fig. 1e). A ~200-nm NbOI flake is excited at normal incidence, and the generated SHG, THG, fourth (FOHG, 4th), fifth (FIHG, 5th), sixth (SIHG, 6th), seventh (SEHG, 7th), eighth (EIHG, 8th), nineth (NIHG, 9th), tenth (TEHG, 10th), and eleventh (ELHG, 11th) harmonic signals are collected in the transmission direction. Figure 3b presents THG, FOHG, and FIHG spectra under 2500-nm excitation, while Fig. 3c, d display SIHG, SEHG, EIHG, NIHG, TEHG, and ELHG spectra under 3500-nm excitation. Remarkably, the NbOI flake generates SEHG, EIHG, NIHG, TEHG, and ELHG signals that extend beyond its optical bandgap into the UV regime, highlighting its exceptional capability for upconversion photodetection and UV light source.

It is well known that harmonic signals generated in the perturbative regime of nonlinear polarization follow the intensity scaling law15: 𝐼 ∝𝐼𝑛, where 𝐼 and 𝐼 are the intensities of Nth-harmonic signals and excitation laser, N is the harmonic order. We performed power-law fits to the experimental results (Fig. 3e, f, Supplementary Fig. S6a). The generated SHG, THG, FOHG, FIHG, SIHG, SEHG, EIHG, and NIHG intensities follow relations of 𝐼2.1, 𝐼3, 𝐼4.2, 𝐼4.8, 𝐼5.3, 𝐼7.1, 𝐼8.1, and 𝐼8.8 , respectively, indicating multiphoton harmonic processes in the perturbative regime (Fig. 3a)15,37. For the high-order harmonic processes, minor differences between the experimental and theoretical results are attributed to measurement uncertainties and signal instability, primarily arising from additive and shot noise15. Owing to the spectral range limitations of the spectrometer, we employ a 3500 nm laser to excite the high-order harmonic signals. It is noted that the 11th-harmonic signal is close to the noise signal, thus we perform the wavelength-dependent 11th-harmonic process with excitation wavelengths at 3530 nm, 3895 nm, and 4125 nm. The corresponding signals at 320 nm, 354 nm, and 375 nm verify the 11th-harmonic process (Supplementary Fig. S10). The similar phenomenon to THG in Fig. 2f is also found in the 6th-harmonic process, which shows the wavelength-dependent anisotropy (Supplementary Fig. S11).

The conversion efficiency (𝜂 = 𝑃 ⁄𝑃 ) is measured using a calibrated spectrometer (Methods). It is evident that high-order harmonic signals exhibit the lower conversion efficiency, as high-order multiphoton optical processes require the higher excitation intensity38-40 (Fig. 3g). Typically, the EIHG conversion efficiency is as high as 3.5×10-10 at an excitation intensity of 120 GW/cm2 in the perturbative regime, same order to that generated in the CuInP S flake (Supplementary Table S3)15. The FIHG conversion efficiency is in the order of 4×10-8, one order higher than that at the same order in the Si metasurface (Supplementary Table S3)41.

Frequency-mixing for MIR frequency upconversion

Multiphoton high-order harmonic generation driven by a single-beam pump requires high pump intensities due to the intrinsically weak high-order nonlinear susceptibilities, e.g., GaP metamaterial requires an excitation intensity of 0.6 TW/cm2 to generate NIHG signals14. In contrast, nonlinear frequency mixing driven by a two-beam pump can generate multiple colors within the spectral range of HHG signals, benefiting from lower excitation intensities due to the large 𝜒(2) and 𝜒(3) values of NbOI . As illustrated in Fig. 1e, we demonstrate nonlinear frequency mixing via a two-beam excitation scheme (𝜔 at 1030 nm, 𝜔 at 1500-5000 nm). The collinearly propagating pump beams are focused on the sample by a lens (Methods). When two beams (𝜔 at 1030 nm, 𝜔 at 2500 nm) are focused onto a ~100-nm NbOI flake with temporal overlapping, four distinct spectral peaks emerge across the entire visible range. As shown in Fig. 4a, b, the signals are categorized into SFG (𝜔 +𝜔 ) at 730 nm, DFWM (2𝜔 −𝜔 ) at 650 nm, SFM1 (𝜔 +2𝜔 ) at 565 nm, and SFM2 (2𝜔 +𝜔 ) at 430 nm. Notably, the FWM peak exhibits the lower amplitude compared to the sum-frequency generation (SFG) peak, reflecting the higher efficiency of 𝜒(2) mediated frequency mixing process42. Furthermore, we systematically verified the physical origins of these frequency-mixing processes through wavelength- and power-dependent measurements, showing that the output wavelengths scale with the input pump wavelengths, while the corresponding intensities follow the expected nonlinear power dependences. For example, the signal peak at 730 nm shows the linear dependence on the 𝜔 and 𝜔 powers (Supplementary Fig. S12a, b). In a similar manner, 𝜔 power dependent SFM (SFM1 and SFM2) spectra are also measurement (Supplementary Fig. S12c). The blue curve shows the nearly quadratic dependence of the SFM2 (2𝜔 +𝜔 ) intensity on the 𝜔 power. In contrast, the red curve shows the linear dependence of the SFM1 (𝜔 +2𝜔 ) intensity on the 𝜔 power. To further confirm the SFG process in the broadband MIR spectral range, the wavelength dependent SFG is also performed, as shown in Fig. 4c. The SFG wavelength is tuned accordingly by varying the 𝜔 wavelength in the range from 1500 to 5000 nm, confirming the high frequency-mixing performance in the broadband MIR spectral range due to large 𝜒(2) values in the infrared region. It is worth noting that the spectrum with 𝜔 =5000 nm is not symmetric due to the asymmetric pump spectrum, which is derived from frequency chirp from the OPA system (including periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN), mirror, and lens)43 and absorption effect of PPLN44.

Typically, the SFG efficiency at the signal wavelength of 2600 nm is calculated (Fig. 4d). The conversion efficiency (𝜂 = 𝑃 ⁄𝑃 ) reaches the maximum value of 6×10-8 at the signal intensity of 663 MW/cm2, where 𝑃 and 𝑃 are SFG power and MIR signal power, respectively. Considering the power ratio between the SFM2 and SFG processes, the conversion efficiency for SFM2 at 430 nm is estimated to be 8×10-9 at the same signal intensity, nearly one order higher than the signal for SIHG at a pump intensity of 110 GW/cm2, confirming the higher efficiency for frequency mixing11. Correspondingly, the maximum normalized SFG conversion efficiency (𝜂 =𝑃 ⁄(𝑃 𝑃 )) is 6×10-4 W-1, where 𝑃 is the pump power. Polarization angle-dependent SFG and SFM processes are also measured by tuning the polarization of the 𝜔 beam (Supplementary Fig. S12d, e). The two beams are co-polarized parallel to the b-axis of NbOI when the angle is 0°. It can be found that both SFG and SFM peaks show the maximum values, and the signals are negligible when the polarizations of the two beams are perpendicular. This demonstrates the frequency mixing process by two beams and the anisotropic response in NbOI . It is worthing noting that nonlinear conversion efficiencies (such as SHG, THG, and SFG) increase monotonically with the thickness smaller than 200 nm, since the thicknesses used in this work is within the coherence lengths (Supplementary Note S4, Fig. S13, S14). The anisotropies of SHG and THG are nearly independent on the flake thickness as both harmonic intensities increase monotonically for thicknesses up to 200 nm as the excitation polarization is aligned along the b- and c-axes, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S15). In addition, the nonlinear response (e.g., SHG) of NbOI deviates from the expected 𝑁2 scaling with layer number due to interference between surface and bulk contributions29,45,46. In order to provide a comprehensive comparison for different nonlinear optical processes, we measured efficiencies of SHG, SFG, THG, 4th-, 5th-, 6th-, 7th-, and 8th-harmonic processes in the same NbOI flake (~200 nm). The results indicate that the conversion efficiency decreases with increasing harmonic order (Supplementary Fig. S16), as high-order processes require higher excitation intensities15,47.

Broadband MIR upconversion imaging

Given the inferior performance of MIR cameras compared to their NIR and visible counterparts, the development of upconversion imaging techniques has become increasingly essential. A promising approach to upconversion imaging involves leveraging strong light-matter interactions in subwavelength resonators arranged into resonant metasurfaces12,48,49. Although metasurface platforms offer exciting opportunities for miniaturized frequency conversion devices without the phase-matching constraints of bulk crystals, they still face limitations, which include reduced power conversion efficiency due to high-order diffraction effects, angle-dependent resonance characteristics across the imaging field of view49. Consequently, there is a pressing need to explore alternative miniature upconversion devices that are simpler to implement and offer imaging performance comparable to their counterparts.

With the broadband and efficient upconversion capability of NbOI established, we demonstrate its application for room-temperature MIR upconversion imaging in Fig. 5. For the SFG process, 1030 nm and MIR light are used as the pump and signal, respectively. In the imaging setup (Fig. 5a), the beam sizes of the pump and signal are controlled by lens groups to approximately 105 μm and 70 μm (Supplementary Note S3, Fig. S17). The 1030 nm light passes through two lenses with different focal lengths (𝑓 = 200 mm and 𝑓 = 30 mm) and directly illuminates the surface of the NbOI flake. For the MIR light, the test target is positioned at the front focal plane of the first lens. The separation between the two lenses is set equal to the sum of their focal lengths, ensuring a conjugate imaging configuration. This configuration allows the MIR beam to be focused onto the same spot on the sample surface, thereby achieving optimal spatial overlap between the laser beams. An objective is placed behind the sample to collect the signals generated by the interaction. To isolate the SFG signal and remove other unwanted signals, two filters (FELH0700 and FESH0875, Thorlabs) are positioned in the signal collection path. Finally, the converted images of the test target are captured by a visible silicon camera (CS135MUM, Thorlabs) at the collection side.

We successfully realized and demonstrated broadband MIR upconversion imaging based on the SFG process in the NbOI crystal. Under white light illumination, the target image is shown in Fig. 5b. Figure 5c displays the SFG converted images captured by the camera for excitation light pairs of 1030 nm+2700 nm, 1030 nm+3500 nm, and 1030 nm+4000 nm, respectively. Notably, the demonstrated SFG imaging technique can, in principle, be extended to arbitrary objects. It is worth noting that upconversion images from different wavelength combinations do not spatially overlap but show vertical offsets. The offsets mainly come from optical misalignments, which arise from the operation mechanism of the OPA system and the external collimation optics. Leveraging the polarization-dependent properties of the SHG process in NbOI , we further demonstrate SHG imaging with different polarizations of the incident beam (1550 nm in this work), as shown in Fig. 5e. Figure 5d shows the target image (the letter "i") under white light illumination. The converted images at polarization angles of 0º, 30º, 50º, and 90º are shown in Fig. 5e. It is evident that the SHG imaging performance deteriorates as the polarization angle of the incident shifts from 0º to 90º. This is because when the polarization aligns with the b-axis of NbOI (0º in our experiment), the SHG efficiency is maximized, resulting in the clearest converted image. As the polarization angle continues to rotate, the misalignment between the excitation beam and the sample's b-axis increases, resulting in reduced conversion efficiency and degraded imaging performance.

## Methods

Synthesis of NbOI crystals and sample preparation

High-quality NbOI bulk crystals were synthesized by the chemical vapor transport method. The reaction precursors Nb, Nb O and I powders with a molar mass ration of 3:1:6 was mixed and sealed in an evacuated quartz tube with pressure less than 10 mbar. The tube was then slowly heated up to 700 °C and maintained at this temperature for 5 days, followed by naturally cooling to room temperature. Finally, the synthesized NbOI crystals were soaked in alcohol to remove the excess I . The NbOI flakes were obtained by mechanical exfoliation from the bulk NbOI .

Electron and phonon characterization

High resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) imaging was carried out on an JEOL 2200FS transmission electron microscope operated at 200 keV. Raman spectra were acquired using a micro-Raman spectrometer (WITec) with a confocal backscattering geometry. A continuous wave 532 nm laser was focused on the samples by an objective lens (×100, NA=0.9) with a spot size of ~1 μm. The generated Raman signals were collected by the same objective and analyzed by a spectrometer equipped with a thermoelectric cooling (TEC) detector. To reveal the phonon anisotropy, the polarization-resolved Raman spectra were measured with the excitation polarization along b- and c-axes, respectively.

Absorbance measurement

The micro-absorption measurement was performed using a Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer (FTIR) with a microscope, in which the NbOI samples were placed between aligned objective lenses for light focusing and collecting. A broadband light source was focused on the sample by an objective lens. The transmitted light was collected by the other one objective lens and then sent to the FTIR. The absorption spectra could be obtained by comparing the transmitted spectra between the sample and the substrate. For measurements of anisotropic absorption spectra in the infrared region, a linear polarizer was set in front of the first objective to realize linearly polarized incidence. Polarized absorption spectra were obtained by making the polarizer along b- and c-axes, respectively.

Nonlinear optical response measurements

The nonlinear optical response of the NbOI flake was measured in the home-built optical system (Fig. 1e). An optical parametric amplifier (OPA) pumped by a mode-locked laser (1030 nm, 400 fs, 100 kHz) was used as the tunable laser source for the nonlinear optical experiments. The excitation beam was focused by an objective lens onto the sample. The transmitted nonlinear signals were collected by another objective lens and analyzed by a spectrometer. To measure the efficiencies, wavelength-dependent and broadband nonlinear optical processes, we used a single or broadband light source to calibrate the collecting path by characterizing the wavelength-dependent losses of the optical setup, including the absorption of the objective, the lens, the fiber, the grating efficiency, and the CCD quantum efficiency. To perform the multiphoton harmonic generations, the MIR incident light was focused by a 40× reflective objective onto the sample, and the generated signals were collected by a 20× objective. To carried out frequency mixing experiments, a near-infrared laser at 1030 nm and another infrared laser (1500-5000 nm) from OPA were spatially combined by a dichroic mirror (DM) and then collinearly propagate into a lens. The temporal overlap between the pulses was controlled by a variable delay line. The generated signals were collected by a 20× objective and then analyzed by a spectrometer.

To measure SHG with parallel and perpendicular configurations, a half waveplate (HWP) and a polarizer were rotated simultaneously to detect SHG signal with the polarization components parallel or perpendicular to the excitation polarization. For anisotropic THG measurement, we rotated a HWP to tune the excitation polarization while keeping the polarizer along c- or b-axes of the NbOI crystal, and thus x- or y-components of the THG signal could be measured. For SHG/THG imaging of the NbOI flake, 1400 nm/1300 nm lasers were used as excitation sources. The samples were scanned with an area of 80 μm×80 μm through a high-resolution X-Y stage, and the SHG/THG signals were detected by a photomultiplier (PMT). We used HWP to tune the excitation polarization. All the measurements were performed in ambient condition, which proves its good stability in the ambient. Long-term stability measurement under 1550-nm excitation indicates that the NbOI crystal can maintain a relatively good quality over a period of 24 h (Supplementary Fig. S18).

This mechanical translation of the crystal, combined with minor wedge angles or non-parallelism relative to the optical axis, introduces a minute but detectable change in the beam’s propagation vector.
Chromatic aberration: The refractive index of the collimating and focusing lenses (e.g., CaF ) is wavelength-dependent. As the MIR wavelength is tuned (e.g., from 3 μm to 4 μm), the effective focal length changes slightly. Residual chromatic aberration results in a slight variation of the focal spot position on the sample plane for non-normal incidence rays.
(2) Phase-matching considerations: In bulk nonlinear crystals, phase-matching imposes a strict angular selection. However, for the ultra-thin NbOI flakes used in our work (thickness L<<coherence length), the longitudinal phase-matching condition is significantly relaxed.

Additionally, the birefringence leads to a walk-off effect where the Poynting vector deviates from the wave vector. However, given the atomic-scale thickness of our samples (typically tens of nanometers), the lateral beam displacement caused by refraction and walk-off within the material is negligible (sub-nanometer scale) compared to the micron-scale shift induced by the external optical path. ## Paper

## Abstract

Nonlinear frequency upconversion of mid-infrared (MIR) light is of particular importance for infrared imaging, detection and spectroscopy. However, achieving efficient and broadband MIR upconversion is hindered by phase-matching constraints and limited nonlinear coefficients of optical materials. Here, we demonstrate phase-matching-free, broadband and efficient multiphoton frequency upconversion in NbOI . We observe generation of harmonics from the second to the 11th order, with upconverted signals spanning from the MIR to the ultraviolet. We also achieve nonlinear frequency mixing in the broad spectral window of 1500-5000 nm, including degenerate four-wave mixing, sum-frequency mixing and sum-frequency generation with an efficiency up to 6×10-⁴ W-¹, surpassing those of leading metasurface-based platforms. Finally, we demonstrate broadband MIR upconversion imaging by direct detection from a conventional silicon camera. Our results establish NbOI as a promising platform for MIR nanophotonics, enabling advanced applications in ultrabroadband imaging, sensing and spectral conversion.

---

## Introduction

Mid-infrared nonlinear optics is crucial for developing next-generation infrared light sources1, enabling ultrasensitive molecular detection2, and advancing on-chip photonic integration3. In particular, multiphoton nonlinear frequency upconversion manifested as second-harmonic generation (SHG)4, third-harmonic generation (THG)5,6, sum-frequency generation (SFG)7,8, difference-frequency generation (DFG)9,10, four-wave mixing (FWM)11,12, and high-order harmonic generation (HHG)13-15, offers an essential route to convert invisible MIR signals into the visible and ultraviolet (UV) ranges for cost-effective and efficient detection and imaging16-18.

Conventional bulk nonlinear materials such as silicon (Si), silicon nitride (Si N ), silicon dioxide (SiO ), and lithium niobate face intrinsic limitations in MIR upconversion due to weak nonlinear susceptibilities, stringent phase-matching requirements, and processing constraints. In contrast, Van der Waals two dimensional (2D) materials, such as graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), exhibit strong optical nonlinearities19,20 that make them attractive for on-chip nonlinear optical devices21,22. However, the nonlinear conversion efficiency (e.g., SHG) in many 2D layered materials is constrained by the layer number, owing to strong interlayer coupling or changes in crystal symmetry, as observed in 2H-TMDCs23, rhombohedral boron nitride (rBN)24,25, SnP Se 16, and 3R-MoS 26,27.

Recently, ferroelectric van der Waals materials such as NbOX (X=I, Cl, Br) have emerged as promising nonlinear platforms due to their intrinsic inversion symmetry breaking and robust optical anisotropy28-33. In particular, NbOI demonstrates exceptionally strong SHG in the visible and near-infrared regions, enhanced by excitonic resonances, and the density functional theory (DFT) predicts an large second-order susceptibilities (𝜒(2)) in the infrared region28. Yet, its potential for broadband multiphoton frequency conversion and parametric processes in the MIR and UV has remained largely unexplored.

Here, we present a comprehensive demonstration of broadband, efficient, and phase-matching-free MIR multiphoton harmonic generation in nanoscale NbOI crystals. We report high-order harmonic generation up to the 11th order, encompassing both even and odd harmonics, with harmonic signals extending deep into UV, enabled by the material’s large 𝜒(2) and 𝜒(3) values (𝜒(2)≈147 pm/V at 1300 nm, ≈121 pm/V at 1700 nm, ≈60 pm/V at 2500 nm, and 𝜒(3)≈3×10-¹⁹ m²/V² at 1550 nm). Beyond harmonic generation, we achieve broadband nonlinear frequency mixing including SFG, degenerate four-wave mixing (DFWM), sum-frequency mixing (SFM), covering a wide input range (1500-5000 nm) with a SFG efficiency up to 6×10-⁴ W-¹ at 2600 nm, surpassing those reported for the state-of-the-art metasurfaces. Particularly, we demonstrate the broadband MIR upconversion imaging (2700-4000 nm) using the visible silicon camera based on phase-matching-free SFG in a single NbOI flake at room temperature. Our findings pave the way for a new paradigm in MIR nonlinear photonics, combining broadband response, large optical nonlinearity, and structural scalability to enable unprecedented capabilities in broadband upconversion, optical imaging, and long-wavelength infrared detection.

---

## Results

Figure 1a illustrates a schematic diagram of MIR upconversion processes in the NbOI flake. Bulk NbOI crystals belong to the monoclinic space group C2 and feature a characteristic van der Waals layered structure along the a-axis (Fig. 1b)28. Figure 1c presents an optical image and an atomic force microscopic image (AFM) of the NbOI flake with a typical thickness of ~8 nm. Atomic-resolved annular dark field-scanning transmission electron microscopy (ADF-STEM) technique confirms the b-axis of the NbOI crystal, consistent with the simulated image (Supplementary Fig. S1c). While NbOI crystals exhibit anisotropic absorption along the two in-plane axes28, no experimental data on absorption in the MIR region was previously available. We measured the absorption spectra of a 20-nm NbOI flake, revealing smooth absorption across a 1000 to 2600 nm spectral range. Notably, the absorption exhibits strong anisotropy in the infrared region (Fig. 1d), attributed to excitonic-absorption-induced decay differences along the two in-plane axes in the visible spectral region28. The difference in the Raman spectra along the b- and c-axes also indicates the anisotropic phonon response derived from different crystal orientations between the two axes (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Strong SHG and THG processes with polarization anisotropy in asymmetric NbOI crystals

We investigate the second- and third-order nonlinear effects of the NbOI crystal in the infrared region through SHG and THG processes (Fig. 2a). The second- and third-order nonlinear susceptibilities of NbOI are quantitatively determined to characterize its nonlinear optical properties. The 𝜒(2) values of the NbOI crystal are calculated to be 147 pm/V at 1300 nm and 121 pm/V at 1700 nm by comparing with quartz (Supplementary Fig. S3). The 𝜒(2) value at 2500 nm is estimated to be ~60 pm/V. The 𝜒(3) values of the NbOI crystal are calculated to be 3×10-19 m2/V2 and 5.5×10-19 m2/V2 at 1550 nm by comparing with the silica substrate and monolayer WS , respectively (Supplementary Fig. S4). The difference in 𝜒(3) is mainly derived from the discrepancies in experimentally reported 𝜒(3) values for TEMDC monolayers. In addition, 𝜒(3) is also independent on the excitation intensity, indicating that extracted 𝜒(3) is not affected by thermal nonlinear optical effects (Supplementary Fig. S5). The SHG (𝜂 = 𝐼 ⁄𝐼 ) and THG (𝜂 = 𝐼 ⁄𝐼 ) conversion efficiencies as a function of the excitation intensity are shown in Fig. 2b. The SHG conversion efficiency under 2500-nm excitation is calculated to be 4.3×10-6 under an excitation intensity of 70 GW/cm2, corresponding to a normalized conversion efficiency (𝜂 ) of 8.6×10-4 W-1 based on the equation34,35: 𝜂 = 𝐼 ⁄𝐼 2. This value is comparable to that of Weyl Te in the MIR region35 and is an order of magnitude higher than that achieved in lithium niobate waveguides34.

The NbOI crystal also exhibits polarization-dependent SHG and THG responses, arising from its intrinsically asymmetric in-plane crystal structure. We introduce the anisotropic ratio (𝜌) to characterize the anisotropic nonlinear optical response of the NbOI crystal. The SHG anisotropic ratio of the NbOI crystal is defined as: 𝜌 = 𝐼 ⁄𝐼 ∝(𝜒 (2) ⁄𝜒 (2) )2 , where 𝐼 is the SHG intensity with the excitation polarization along the (c) x-axis, 𝐼 is the SHG intensity with the excitation polarization along the (b) y-axis. Figure 2c demonstrates polar plot of the SHG intensity under 2500-nm excitation with both parallel and perpendicular configurations. The SHG response demonstrates distinct in-plane anisotropy, with the maximum intensity observed along the b-axis. This observation is well explained and fitted through crystal symmetry analysis of the NbOI crystal (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Note S2). The 𝜌 value at 2500 nm is ~14, corresponding to 𝜒 :𝜒 =3.7. The differences in 𝜌 across different wavelengths arise from the dispersion of the nonlinear optical susceptibility in the NbOI crystal (Fig. 2e, Supplementary Fig. 6b, c, Fig. S9)28. Supplementary Fig. S8a-c show SHG mappings of the NbOI flake at 1400 nm along the b- and c-axes, respectively. Notably, a strong SHG signal is observed when the excitation polarization is along the b-axis, whereas the SHG signal is negligible when the excitation polarization is along the c-axis.

The THG anisotropic ratio is defined as: 𝜌 = 𝐼 ⁄ 𝐼 ∝(𝜒 (3) ⁄𝜒 (3) )2 . Figure 2d demonstrates x- and y- components of the THG intensity under 2500-nm excitation. It can be found that THG intensity is the largest when the excitation polarization is along the b-axis. The extracted relative magnitudes of the 𝜒(3) tensor components are 𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) =1:1.6:0.05:0.2, corresponding to 𝜌 =2.56. THG shows different polar-plot patterns under 1300-nm and 1550-nm excitations due to the 𝜒(3) dispersion (Supplementary Fig. S7). The extracted relative magnitudes of the 𝜒(3) tensor components are 𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) =1:3.2:0.9:0.1 at 1300 nm corresponding to 𝜌 =10 and 𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) :𝜒 (3) =1:0.8:0.9:0.1 at 1550 nm corresponding to 𝜌 =0.64. The mapping intensity in Fig. S8e is larger than that in Fig. S8f, confirming strong THG anisotropy at 1300 nm. This mapping technique enables effective identification of the crystal axes in large-area NbOI flakes. The 𝜌 value of ~17 is higher than that observed in most reported 2D layered materials (Supplementary Table S2).

High-order harmonic processes

Due to the inversion symmetry breaking caused by spontaneous ferroelectric polarization in the bulk state, even-order harmonic processes (such as SHG, SFG, 4th-, and 6th-harmonic processes in the MIR region) can be potentially realized in the NbOI flake28,36. The high-order multiphoton optical processes in NbOI flakes are investigated based on a home-built optical system (Fig. 1e). A ~200-nm NbOI flake is excited at normal incidence, and the generated SHG, THG, fourth (FOHG, 4th), fifth (FIHG, 5th), sixth (SIHG, 6th), seventh (SEHG, 7th), eighth (EIHG, 8th), nineth (NIHG, 9th), tenth (TEHG, 10th), and eleventh (ELHG, 11th) harmonic signals are collected in the transmission direction. Figure 3b presents THG, FOHG, and FIHG spectra under 2500-nm excitation, while Fig. 3c, d display SIHG, SEHG, EIHG, NIHG, TEHG, and ELHG spectra under 3500-nm excitation. Remarkably, the NbOI flake generates SEHG, EIHG, NIHG, TEHG, and ELHG signals that extend beyond its optical bandgap into the UV regime, highlighting its exceptional capability for upconversion photodetection and UV light source.

It is well known that harmonic signals generated in the perturbative regime of nonlinear polarization follow the intensity scaling law15: 𝐼 ∝𝐼𝑛, where 𝐼 and 𝐼 are the intensities of Nth-harmonic signals and excitation laser, N is the harmonic order. We performed power-law fits to the experimental results (Fig. 3e, f, Supplementary Fig. S6a). The generated SHG, THG, FOHG, FIHG, SIHG, SEHG, EIHG, and NIHG intensities follow relations of 𝐼2.1, 𝐼3, 𝐼4.2, 𝐼4.8, 𝐼5.3, 𝐼7.1, 𝐼8.1, and 𝐼8.8 , respectively, indicating multiphoton harmonic processes in the perturbative regime (Fig. 3a)15,37. For the high-order harmonic processes, minor differences between the experimental and theoretical results are attributed to measurement uncertainties and signal instability, primarily arising from additive and shot noise15. Owing to the spectral range limitations of the spectrometer, we employ a 3500 nm laser to excite the high-order harmonic signals. It is noted that the 11th-harmonic signal is close to the noise signal, thus we perform the wavelength-dependent 11th-harmonic process with excitation wavelengths at 3530 nm, 3895 nm, and 4125 nm. The corresponding signals at 320 nm, 354 nm, and 375 nm verify the 11th-harmonic process (Supplementary Fig. S10). The similar phenomenon to THG in Fig. 2f is also found in the 6th-harmonic process, which shows the wavelength-dependent anisotropy (Supplementary Fig. S11).

The conversion efficiency (𝜂 = 𝑃 ⁄𝑃 ) is measured using a calibrated spectrometer (Methods). It is evident that high-order harmonic signals exhibit the lower conversion efficiency, as high-order multiphoton optical processes require the higher excitation intensity38-40 (Fig. 3g). Typically, the EIHG conversion efficiency is as high as 3.5×10-10 at an excitation intensity of 120 GW/cm2 in the perturbative regime, same order to that generated in the CuInP S flake (Supplementary Table S3)15. The FIHG conversion efficiency is in the order of 4×10-8, one order higher than that at the same order in the Si metasurface (Supplementary Table S3)41.

Frequency-mixing for MIR frequency upconversion

Multiphoton high-order harmonic generation driven by a single-beam pump requires high pump intensities due to the intrinsically weak high-order nonlinear susceptibilities, e.g., GaP metamaterial requires an excitation intensity of 0.6 TW/cm2 to generate NIHG signals14. In contrast, nonlinear frequency mixing driven by a two-beam pump can generate multiple colors within the spectral range of HHG signals, benefiting from lower excitation intensities due to the large 𝜒(2) and 𝜒(3) values of NbOI . As illustrated in Fig. 1e, we demonstrate nonlinear frequency mixing via a two-beam excitation scheme (𝜔 at 1030 nm, 𝜔 at 1500-5000 nm). The collinearly propagating pump beams are focused on the sample by a lens (Methods). When two beams (𝜔 at 1030 nm, 𝜔 at 2500 nm) are focused onto a ~100-nm NbOI flake with temporal overlapping, four distinct spectral peaks emerge across the entire visible range. As shown in Fig. 4a, b, the signals are categorized into SFG (𝜔 +𝜔 ) at 730 nm, DFWM (2𝜔 −𝜔 ) at 650 nm, SFM1 (𝜔 +2𝜔 ) at 565 nm, and SFM2 (2𝜔 +𝜔 ) at 430 nm. Notably, the FWM peak exhibits the lower amplitude compared to the sum-frequency generation (SFG) peak, reflecting the higher efficiency of 𝜒(2) mediated frequency mixing process42. Furthermore, we systematically verified the physical origins of these frequency-mixing processes through wavelength- and power-dependent measurements, showing that the output wavelengths scale with the input pump wavelengths, while the corresponding intensities follow the expected nonlinear power dependences. For example, the signal peak at 730 nm shows the linear dependence on the 𝜔 and 𝜔 powers (Supplementary Fig. S12a, b). In a similar manner, 𝜔 power dependent SFM (SFM1 and SFM2) spectra are also measurement (Supplementary Fig. S12c). The blue curve shows the nearly quadratic dependence of the SFM2 (2𝜔 +𝜔 ) intensity on the 𝜔 power. In contrast, the red curve shows the linear dependence of the SFM1 (𝜔 +2𝜔 ) intensity on the 𝜔 power. To further confirm the SFG process in the broadband MIR spectral range, the wavelength dependent SFG is also performed, as shown in Fig. 4c. The SFG wavelength is tuned accordingly by varying the 𝜔 wavelength in the range from 1500 to 5000 nm, confirming the high frequency-mixing performance in the broadband MIR spectral range due to large 𝜒(2) values in the infrared region. It is worth noting that the spectrum with 𝜔 =5000 nm is not symmetric due to the asymmetric pump spectrum, which is derived from frequency chirp from the OPA system (including periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN), mirror, and lens)43 and absorption effect of PPLN44.

Typically, the SFG efficiency at the signal wavelength of 2600 nm is calculated (Fig. 4d). The conversion efficiency (𝜂 = 𝑃 ⁄𝑃 ) reaches the maximum value of 6×10-8 at the signal intensity of 663 MW/cm2, where 𝑃 and 𝑃 are SFG power and MIR signal power, respectively. Considering the power ratio between the SFM2 and SFG processes, the conversion efficiency for SFM2 at 430 nm is estimated to be 8×10-9 at the same signal intensity, nearly one order higher than the signal for SIHG at a pump intensity of 110 GW/cm2, confirming the higher efficiency for frequency mixing11. Correspondingly, the maximum normalized SFG conversion efficiency (𝜂 =𝑃 ⁄(𝑃 𝑃 )) is 6×10-4 W-1, where 𝑃 is the pump power. Polarization angle-dependent SFG and SFM processes are also measured by tuning the polarization of the 𝜔 beam (Supplementary Fig. S12d, e). The two beams are co-polarized parallel to the b-axis of NbOI when the angle is 0°. It can be found that both SFG and SFM peaks show the maximum values, and the signals are negligible when the polarizations of the two beams are perpendicular. This demonstrates the frequency mixing process by two beams and the anisotropic response in NbOI . It is worthing noting that nonlinear conversion efficiencies (such as SHG, THG, and SFG) increase monotonically with the thickness smaller than 200 nm, since the thicknesses used in this work is within the coherence lengths (Supplementary Note S4, Fig. S13, S14). The anisotropies of SHG and THG are nearly independent on the flake thickness as both harmonic intensities increase monotonically for thicknesses up to 200 nm as the excitation polarization is aligned along the b- and c-axes, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S15). In addition, the nonlinear response (e.g., SHG) of NbOI deviates from the expected 𝑁2 scaling with layer number due to interference between surface and bulk contributions29,45,46. In order to provide a comprehensive comparison for different nonlinear optical processes, we measured efficiencies of SHG, SFG, THG, 4th-, 5th-, 6th-, 7th-, and 8th-harmonic processes in the same NbOI flake (~200 nm). The results indicate that the conversion efficiency decreases with increasing harmonic order (Supplementary Fig. S16), as high-order processes require higher excitation intensities15,47.

Broadband MIR upconversion imaging

Given the inferior performance of MIR cameras compared to their NIR and visible counterparts, the development of upconversion imaging techniques has become increasingly essential. A promising approach to upconversion imaging involves leveraging strong light-matter interactions in subwavelength resonators arranged into resonant metasurfaces12,48,49. Although metasurface platforms offer exciting opportunities for miniaturized frequency conversion devices without the phase-matching constraints of bulk crystals, they still face limitations, which include reduced power conversion efficiency due to high-order diffraction effects, angle-dependent resonance characteristics across the imaging field of view49. Consequently, there is a pressing need to explore alternative miniature upconversion devices that are simpler to implement and offer imaging performance comparable to their counterparts.

With the broadband and efficient upconversion capability of NbOI established, we demonstrate its application for room-temperature MIR upconversion imaging in Fig. 5. For the SFG process, 1030 nm and MIR light are used as the pump and signal, respectively. In the imaging setup (Fig. 5a), the beam sizes of the pump and signal are controlled by lens groups to approximately 105 μm and 70 μm (Supplementary Note S3, Fig. S17). The 1030 nm light passes through two lenses with different focal lengths (𝑓 = 200 mm and 𝑓 = 30 mm) and directly illuminates the surface of the NbOI flake. For the MIR light, the test target is positioned at the front focal plane of the first lens. The separation between the two lenses is set equal to the sum of their focal lengths, ensuring a conjugate imaging configuration. This configuration allows the MIR beam to be focused onto the same spot on the sample surface, thereby achieving optimal spatial overlap between the laser beams. An objective is placed behind the sample to collect the signals generated by the interaction. To isolate the SFG signal and remove other unwanted signals, two filters (FELH0700 and FESH0875, Thorlabs) are positioned in the signal collection path. Finally, the converted images of the test target are captured by a visible silicon camera (CS135MUM, Thorlabs) at the collection side.

We successfully realized and demonstrated broadband MIR upconversion imaging based on the SFG process in the NbOI crystal. Under white light illumination, the target image is shown in Fig. 5b. Figure 5c displays the SFG converted images captured by the camera for excitation light pairs of 1030 nm+2700 nm, 1030 nm+3500 nm, and 1030 nm+4000 nm, respectively. Notably, the demonstrated SFG imaging technique can, in principle, be extended to arbitrary objects. It is worth noting that upconversion images from different wavelength combinations do not spatially overlap but show vertical offsets. The offsets mainly come from optical misalignments, which arise from the operation mechanism of the OPA system and the external collimation optics. Leveraging the polarization-dependent properties of the SHG process in NbOI , we further demonstrate SHG imaging with different polarizations of the incident beam (1550 nm in this work), as shown in Fig. 5e. Figure 5d shows the target image (the letter "i") under white light illumination. The converted images at polarization angles of 0º, 30º, 50º, and 90º are shown in Fig. 5e. It is evident that the SHG imaging performance deteriorates as the polarization angle of the incident shifts from 0º to 90º. This is because when the polarization aligns with the b-axis of NbOI (0º in our experiment), the SHG efficiency is maximized, resulting in the clearest converted image. As the polarization angle continues to rotate, the misalignment between the excitation beam and the sample's b-axis increases, resulting in reduced conversion efficiency and degraded imaging performance.

## Methods

Synthesis of NbOI crystals and sample preparation

High-quality NbOI bulk crystals were synthesized by the chemical vapor transport method. The reaction precursors Nb, Nb O and I powders with a molar mass ration of 3:1:6 was mixed and sealed in an evacuated quartz tube with pressure less than 10 mbar. The tube was then slowly heated up to 700 °C and maintained at this temperature for 5 days, followed by naturally cooling to room temperature. Finally, the synthesized NbOI crystals were soaked in alcohol to remove the excess I . The NbOI flakes were obtained by mechanical exfoliation from the bulk NbOI .

Electron and phonon characterization

High resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) imaging was carried out on an JEOL 2200FS transmission electron microscope operated at 200 keV. Raman spectra were acquired using a micro-Raman spectrometer (WITec) with a confocal backscattering geometry. A continuous wave 532 nm laser was focused on the samples by an objective lens (×100, NA=0.9) with a spot size of ~1 μm. The generated Raman signals were collected by the same objective and analyzed by a spectrometer equipped with a thermoelectric cooling (TEC) detector. To reveal the phonon anisotropy, the polarization-resolved Raman spectra were measured with the excitation polarization along b- and c-axes, respectively.

Absorbance measurement

The micro-absorption measurement was performed using a Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer (FTIR) with a microscope, in which the NbOI samples were placed between aligned objective lenses for light focusing and collecting. A broadband light source was focused on the sample by an objective lens. The transmitted light was collected by the other one objective lens and then sent to the FTIR. The absorption spectra could be obtained by comparing the transmitted spectra between the sample and the substrate. For measurements of anisotropic absorption spectra in the infrared region, a linear polarizer was set in front of the first objective to realize linearly polarized incidence. Polarized absorption spectra were obtained by making the polarizer along b- and c-axes, respectively.

Nonlinear optical response measurements

The nonlinear optical response of the NbOI flake was measured in the home-built optical system (Fig. 1e). An optical parametric amplifier (OPA) pumped by a mode-locked laser (1030 nm, 400 fs, 100 kHz) was used as the tunable laser source for the nonlinear optical experiments. The excitation beam was focused by an objective lens onto the sample. The transmitted nonlinear signals were collected by another objective lens and analyzed by a spectrometer. To measure the efficiencies, wavelength-dependent and broadband nonlinear optical processes, we used a single or broadband light source to calibrate the collecting path by characterizing the wavelength-dependent losses of the optical setup, including the absorption of the objective, the lens, the fiber, the grating efficiency, and the CCD quantum efficiency. To perform the multiphoton harmonic generations, the MIR incident light was focused by a 40× reflective objective onto the sample, and the generated signals were collected by a 20× objective. To carried out frequency mixing experiments, a near-infrared laser at 1030 nm and another infrared laser (1500-5000 nm) from OPA were spatially combined by a dichroic mirror (DM) and then collinearly propagate into a lens. The temporal overlap between the pulses was controlled by a variable delay line. The generated signals were collected by a 20× objective and then analyzed by a spectrometer.

To measure SHG with parallel and perpendicular configurations, a half waveplate (HWP) and a polarizer were rotated simultaneously to detect SHG signal with the polarization components parallel or perpendicular to the excitation polarization. For anisotropic THG measurement, we rotated a HWP to tune the excitation polarization while keeping the polarizer along c- or b-axes of the NbOI crystal, and thus x- or y-components of the THG signal could be measured. For SHG/THG imaging of the NbOI flake, 1400 nm/1300 nm lasers were used as excitation sources. The samples were scanned with an area of 80 μm×80 μm through a high-resolution X-Y stage, and the SHG/THG signals were detected by a photomultiplier (PMT). We used HWP to tune the excitation polarization. All the measurements were performed in ambient condition, which proves its good stability in the ambient. Long-term stability measurement under 1550-nm excitation indicates that the NbOI crystal can maintain a relatively good quality over a period of 24 h (Supplementary Fig. S18).

6- In Fig. 5c, upconversion images from different wavelength combinations do not spatially overlap but show vertical offsets. The possible causes, such as phase-matching, optical alignment, or material anisotropy, should be discussed.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this keen observation and the opportunity to clarify the physical mechanisms governing the spatial stability of the excitation beam. We agree that the slight spatial displacement of the MIR beam during wavelength tuning is a critical factor for imaging registration. We have carefully analyzed this phenomenon based on the three suggested aspects: (1) Optical alignment & Beam pointing, (2) Phase-matching conditions, and (3) Material anisotropy.
Our analysis reveals that the shift is primarily attributed to the inherent beam pointing characteristics of the OPA system and chromatic aberration in the external optics, while material-induced effects are present but secondary due to the ultrathin nature of the sample.
(1) Optical alignment and beam pointing stability: The primary source of the observed spatial shift originates from the operation mechanism of the OPA system and the external collimation optics:
PPLN period switching: To cover the broad mid-infrared spectral range, our OPA system requires switching between different poling periods of the PPLN crystal. This mechanical translation of the crystal, combined with minor wedge angles or non-parallelism relative to the optical axis, introduces a minute but detectable change in the beam’s propagation vector.
Chromatic aberration: The refractive index of the collimating and focusing lenses (e.g., CaF ) is wavelength-dependent. As the MIR wavelength is tuned (e.g., from 3 μm to 4 μm), the effective focal length changes slightly. Residual chromatic aberration results in a slight variation of the focal spot position on the sample plane for non-normal incidence rays.
(2) Phase-matching considerations: In bulk nonlinear crystals, phase-matching imposes a strict angular selection. However, for the ultra-thin NbOI flakes used in our work (thickness L<<coherence length), the longitudinal phase-matching condition is significantly relaxed.
Spatial overlap sensitivity: While the thin film allows for broadband up-conversion without strict angle tuning, the conversion efficiency is strictly confined to the spatial overlap region between the pump and the signal beams. The "shift" observed in the up-converted image is, therefore, a direct mapping of the MIR probe beam's displacement (discussed in point 1) relative to the fixed pump beam. The relaxed phase-matching ensures that the signal is still generated despite these small angular deviations, but it does not correct the spatial position.
(3) Material anisotropy and dispersion: We also considered the intrinsic properties of the NbOI material:
Dispersion & Birefringence: NbOI exhibits strong optical anisotropy. According to Snell’s Law, the refraction angle inside the material changes with wavelength due to dispersion. Additionally, the birefringence leads to a walk-off effect where the Poynting vector deviates from the wave vector. However, given the atomic-scale thickness of our samples (typically tens of nanometers), the lateral beam displacement caused by refraction and walk-off within the material is negligible (sub-nanometer scale) compared to the micron-scale shift induced by the external optical path. Therefore, while anisotropy is a fundamental property of NbOI , it is not the dominant cause of the macroscopic spot shift observed in the experiment.
